result.title: Sequence-only prediction of VHH nanobody epitopes and paratopes on HER2 with a frozen protein language model ( ESM2) and a structure-derived residue prior
result.authorString: Babu D, Pandurangan S, Agilisium Consulting.
result.abstractText:
Mapping which antigen residues an antibody contacts (the epitope) and which antibody residues do the contacting (the paratope) is central to therapeutic antibody engineering, yet most accurate methods require a solved or predicted three dimensional complex. We address a sequence only formulation: predict the HER2 epitope and the single domain antibody (VHH, or nanobody) paratope from the two sequences alone, with no three dimensional structure prediction at any stage. We pair a frozen ESM2 650M protein language model, used strictly as a feature extractor, with a lightweight trainable module per chain encoders, a shared cross attention block, and epitope, paratope and binder heads (12.2M trainable parameters) trained jointly on three public sources: HER2 binding and blocking competition assays ("AVIDa hHER2" to be published by organizers of SEPIQ 2026 The authors have no right to share the dataset to public ), residue level antibody antigen contacts (SAbDab2), and two reference antibody crystal structures. The blocking competition signal is de confounded into a trastuzumab minus pertuzumab contrast whose sign encodes the HER2 domain and which is used only as a training target, never as a model input. Under a three way, sequence cluster level split with a test set opened exactly once, the binder head reaches PR AUC 0.999 and the paratope head 0.659, while residue level epitope prediction on novel antigens remains near baseline (0.070) a limitation the sealed split exposes rather than hides. Sequence alone recovers the competition derived HER2 domain (the competitor class) for 87.7% of held out clones, a leakage free result. For HER2 specifically, a residue prior built from 25 mined HER2 antibody complexes and validated by leave one out reaches 0.26 to 0.29 residue PR AUC once the domain is correct, roughly 3.6 times the language model head alone. We release and report two submission variants per test clone, a fully sequence only prediction and a competition informed one ,and document which data were used where.

Keywords:

epitope prediction; paratope prediction; nanobody; VHH; HER2; protein language model; ESM2; cross attention; antibody antigen interface; leakage safe evaluation.

result.title: Protein Language Model–Conditioned Graph Neural Networks for Multitask Ligand Activity Prediction Across Human GPCRs
result.authorString: De M, Lodh E, Majumder S, Chowdhury T.
result.abstractText: Predicting ligand activity across G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) requires models that capture both molecular structure and receptor-specific information while remaining robust to chemical and target-domain shift. We developed a multimodal graph neural network that combines explicit ligand molecular graphs with frozen protein language model representations of GPCR sequences and jointly predicts quantitative pActivity and binary activity. The model was trained on 271,739 curated ligand–GPCR pairs spanning 183,694 ligands and 216 human GPCRs and evaluated using random, Bemis–Murcko scaffold, and strict cold-ligand partitions. With ESM-2 650M receptor embeddings, the selected model achieved mean absolute errors of 0.513 ± 0.006, 0.540 ± 0.006, and 0.641 ± 0.005 pActivity units under random, cold-ligand, and scaffold evaluation, respectively, substantially outperforming a protein-aware fixed-feature multilayer perceptron and consistently improving quantitative prediction over a matched GINE reference. Removing receptor embeddings markedly degraded both regression and classification, whereas differences among ESM-2 35M, ESM-2 650M, and ProtT5 were comparatively small. Independent evaluation on 6,319 ChEMBL 37/BindingDB pairs revealed a substantial external domain shift, with mean absolute error increasing to approximately 0.94–0.95 despite chemically stringent internal validation. Nevertheless, receptor-specific information remained highly informative in a DRD2–DRD3 selectivity analysis: the cold-ligand ensemble achieved  R 2 = 0.853, Spearman  ρ = 0.916, and ROC-AUC = 0.966 for strong DRD3 selectivity, whereas the receptor-independent ablation approached chance-level discrimination. These results establish protein-language-model-conditioned molecular graph learning as a scalable strategy for GPCR bioactivity prediction while identifying chemotype novelty, external-domain transfer, and richer ligand–receptor interaction representations as key remaining challenges.

result.title: CHORUS: A proteome-scale atlas of membrane interaction interfaces constructed using cross-protein language model embeddings from sequences alone
result.authorString: Zhao J, Huang S, Sun J.
result.abstractText: Membrane proteins drive vital cellular signaling and bioenergetics yet resolving their physical interaction interfaces remains hindered by the paucity of experimental complexes and the breakdown of sequence alignments across hydrophobic bilayers. Here, we present CHORUS, a sequence-only deep-learning framework that decodes interaction sites across membrane proteins without requiring 3D structures, multiple sequence alignments (MSAs), or predefined partner identities. By systematically synthesizing complementary latent representations across diverse protein language model (pLM) families and functional layer depths, CHORUS outperforms 18 established sequence- and structure-based methods across 4,655 homology-isolated test contexts (average precision: 0.643), demonstrating amplified predictive capacity within the lipid-embedded core (0.746). We show that CHORUS delineates quaternary contact boundaries across megadalton respiratory supercomplexes directly from sequences alone (0.984). We deliver the CHORUS Atlas (  https://chorus.atlas.sunnylab.org ), providing precomputed, residue-resolved interaction landscapes for 80,619 reviewed transmembrane proteins spanning 4,918 species and 33.7 million residues to empower interactome-scale discovery and allosteric therapeutic design.
